items.title: The Last War Philosophical Insights into the End of Humanity
items.abstract: The history of human civilization has been shaped by war, each conflict etching its legacy into the fabric of existence. Yet, what if the final war, the one that concludes the saga of humanity, is upon us? In this thought-provoking exploration, Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, delves into the philosophical, ethical, and existential implications of humanity’s last war. This book does not merely examine warfare as a strategic or political tool but questions its role in defining human identity. As technological advancements in weaponry accelerate toward an uncontrollable abyss, the line between self-defense and self-destruction blurs. From the ethical dilemmas of nuclear warfare to the digital battlegrounds of the future, every chapter illuminates the fragility of peace and the looming shadow of extinction. By weaving historical analysis, philosophical reflections, and contemporary case studies, this work serves as both a warning and an inquiry. Can war be averted, or is it an inevitable conclusion to human nature? What moral responsibilities do global leaders bear in preventing such devastation? With deep intellectual rigor and an urgent sense of realism, this book invites readers to confront the possibility of the last war—not as a distant nightmare but as a stark reality demanding immediate contemplation. The writing of this book is deeply rooted in the concern that modern warfare has evolved beyond conventional understanding. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, authored this work in response to the alarming trajectory of global conflicts that now intertwine with technological singularity, artificial intelligence, and weapons of unprecedented destruction. Published in 2011, this study aims to dissect the philosophical dimensions of war, highlighting the paradox of progress that brings humanity closer to its ultimate demise. War has long been perceived as a mechanism of power, control, and territorial expansion. However, this book redefines conflict not as an isolated event but as a culmination of human ideologies, fears, and the relentless pursuit of superiority. The discussion extends beyond conventional military strategies, touching upon cyberwarfare, biological weapons, and AI-driven conflicts, emphasizing the urgency of ethical governance over technological advancements. The rapid militarization of space, the increasing automation of warfare, and the unpredictable nature of geopolitical tensions have necessitated a deeper inquiry into the finality of war. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, observed that humanity stands at a critical threshold where the distinction between war and annihilation is vanishing. The rise of unmanned combat systems and autonomous decision-making weapons amplifies the risk of irreversible global catastrophe. The central theme of this book is the philosophical interrogation of war's necessity and its ethical ramifications. Through existentialist and utilitarian perspectives, the book scrutinizes whether human civilization can exist without conflict or if war is embedded in the very essence of human survival. The exploration is not limited to military confrontations but extends to socio-political conflicts, ideological warfare, and economic battles that shape global stability. While wars of the past have followed discernible patterns, modern warfare presents unpredictability fueled by technological dominance. The book identifies economic disparity, resource depletion, and political radicalization as harbingers of the last war. These indicators serve as a warning system for humanity, urging proactive measures before irreversible escalation. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, establishes multiple variables essential for understanding war’s trajectory, including state sovereignty, military-industrial expansion, ethical considerations in AI warfare, and the psychological conditioning of societies toward conflict acceptance. By analyzing these elements, the book constructs a framework to predict and possibly mitigate future large-scale wars. Several key factors drive the discussion within this book: the historical repetition of wars despite peace efforts, the weaponization of emerging technologies, and the philosophical dilemma of whether war is an unavoidable consequence of civilization. The study also considers the role of global governance institutions and their effectiveness in preventing mass destruction. The work presents theoretical and practical approaches to conflict resolution, advocating for diplomatic restructuring, ethical AI governance, and alternative frameworks for international negotiations. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, proposes a shift in global priorities—from military investment to sustainable human development—as a critical strategy in averting global catastrophe. items.title: The Longitudinal Relationship Between Intrinsic Motivation, Grade Motivation and Prosocial Behavior in Chinese Adolescents: A Cross-Lagged Panel Study
items.abstract: Prosocial behavior is crucial for the development of adolescents. Prosocial behavior requires strong internal motivation to drive it, but the prospective association between the two is still unclear. In addition, there is still a gap in the relationship between grade motivation as a unique external motivation and prosocial behavior. To explore the prospective associations between them, we conducted two follow-up surveys (six months apart) on 862 Chinese adolescents (423 boys and 439 girls) to collect data on intrinsic motivation, grade motivation and prosocial behavior (relational prosocial behavior and practical prosocial behavior). The cross-lagged panel study results revealed that intrinsic motivation at T1 was positively associated with relational and practical prosocial behavior at T2. In contrast, grade motivation at T1 was not significantly associated with later prosocial behavior, and prosocial behavior at T1 was not significantly associated with later intrinsic motivation or grade motivation. These findings indicate that intrinsic motivation may be a potential antecedent for prosocial behavior in Chinese adolescents later in life, but the observed associations should be cautiously interpreted.
topics: Child and Adolescent Psychosocial and Emotional Development

items.title: The moderating role of gender and generational cohort on the effects of artificial intelligence usage and learning adaptability on the academic performance of university students in Zimbabwe
items.abstract: This study investigated the moderating role of gender and generational cohorts on the effects of artificial intelligence (AI) usage, learning adaptability, and academic performance of university students in Zimbabwe. Three hundred and twenty-five students at Great Zimbabwe University, Zimbabwe Open University and Women's University in Africa responded to the questionnaires. The study found that AI usage and learning adaptability positively effect academic performance. The study found that generational cohort moderates the effects of AI usage on academic performance, but gender does not. The findings of this research are that gender and generational cohort do not moderate the effects of learning adaptability and academic performance of university students in Zimbabwe. The research implies that students should use AI to enhance their academic performance and develop learning adaptability, which is also key to academic performance.

items.title: The moon’s many faces: A single unified transformer for multimodal lunar reconstruction
items.abstract: Multimodal learning is an emerging research topic across multiple disciplines but has rarely been applied to planetary science. In this contribution, we propose a single, unified transformer architecture trained to learn shared representations between multiple sources like grayscale images, Digital Elevation Models (DEMs), surface normals, and albedo maps. The architecture supports flexible translation from any input modality to any target modality. Our results demonstrate that our foundation model learns physically plausible relations across these four modalities. We further identify that image-based 3D reconstruction and albedo estimation (Shape and Albedo from Shading) of lunar images can be formulated as a multimodal learning problem. Our results demonstrate the potential of multimodal learning to solve Shape and Albedo from Shading and provide a new approach for large-scale planetary 3D reconstruction. Adding more input modalities in the future will further improve the results and enable tasks such as photometric normalization and co-registration.

items.title: The need for verification in artificial intelligence-driven scientific discovery
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming the practice of science. Machine learning (ML) and large language models (LLMs) can generate hypotheses at a scale and speed far exceeding traditional methods, offering the potential to accelerate discovery across diverse fields. However, the abundance of hypotheses introduces a critical challenge; without scalable and reliable mechanisms for verification, scientific progress risks being hindered rather than advanced. In this article, we trace the historical development of scientific discovery, examine how AI is reshaping established practices for discovery and review the principal approaches, ranging from data-driven methods and knowledge-aware neural architectures to symbolic reasoning frameworks and LLM agents. While these systems can uncover patterns and propose candidate laws, their scientific value ultimately depends on rigorous and transparent verification, which we argue must be the cornerstone of AI-assisted discovery. This article is part of the discussion meeting issue 'Symbolic regression in the physical sciences'.

items.title: THE PARADOX OF IRRIGATED FRUIT CULTURE: SOCIOENVIRONMENTAL IMPACTS AND OCCUPATIONAL HEALTH IN THE PETROLINA-JUAZEIRO HUB
items.abstract: The rapid expansion of irrigated fruit production in the Petrolina–Juazeiro hub has positioned the Brazilian semiarid as a strategic agro-export region, while simultaneously intensifying socioenvironmental inequalities and occupational health risks. This paradox reflects a development model in which economic gains coexist with diffuse and often invisible forms of exposure. This study aims to analyze the socioenvironmental and health impacts associated with irrigated agribusiness, focusing on the interaction between chemical exposure, water dynamics, and territorial vulnerability. An integrative literature review was conducted using international and regional databases, complemented by grey literature. A total of 216 records were initially identified and subjected to systematic screening and eligibility procedures. The analysis was structured around three axes: biochemical-clinical, socioeconomic, and geoenvironmental. The results indicate that pesticide exposure in the region is chronic, cumulative, and mediated by environmental and social factors. Evidence shows associations with genotoxicity, endocrine disruption, and underreported chronic diseases, alongside labor precariousness and gender inequality. Contamination pathways extend through soil and water systems, amplifying exposure beyond occupational settings. The discussion reveals that these dynamics are embedded in a broader framework of environmental injustice, where risks are unevenly distributed and structurally produced. The interaction between climate conditions, irrigation systems, and chemical use intensifies exposure, supporting the conceptualization of a chemical-hydric exposome. In conclusion, the study highlights the need for integrated regulatory approaches, improved surveillance systems, and policies that address cumulative exposure and territorial inequalities in semiarid agro-export regions.

items.title: The Political Philosophy of War Propaganda and Its Consequences
items.abstract: War is not merely fought with weapons on the battlefield but is shaped long before the first shot is fired. 2011. The Political Philosophy of War Propaganda and Its Consequences is a profound exploration of how propaganda has been systematically used to manipulate perceptions, justify conflicts, and sustain power structures. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, unveils the intricate relationship between war narratives, state agendas, and the psychological conditioning of societies. Published in 2011 in Geneva, Switzerland, this book critically examines the philosophy underpinning propaganda and its far-reaching implications. The pages unravel historical and contemporary examples of war propaganda, shedding light on how information is weaponized to manufacture consent. Governments, media, and international institutions are dissected as the architects of public opinion, often distorting reality to serve political and economic interests. The book further explores how the United Nations, as a global entity, struggles to navigate these deceptive narratives while attempting to maintain peace and diplomacy. Education is presented as both a battleground and a tool for resistance. The Education Training Centre is examined as a potential counterforce against the institutionalized manipulation of truth. By fostering critical thinking and ethical discourse, societies can reclaim their agency and dismantle the illusions that perpetuate endless cycles of war. This book is a wake-up call—an urgent appeal to question, analyze, and resist the forces that dictate the course of global conflict. The motivation for writing this book arises from the undeniable impact of propaganda in shaping wars and their aftermath. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, seeks to unravel the mechanisms that allow propaganda to thrive and its role in constructing war as a necessary, even heroic, endeavor. The book was published in 2011 in Geneva, Switzerland, a city renowned for its diplomatic engagements and as a hub of international discourse on peace and conflict. History has repeatedly demonstrated that wars are not only fought with military power but also with narratives that legitimize aggression. From ancient empires to modern superpowers, states have mastered the art of persuasion to justify violence, rally populations, and silence opposition. This book challenges these accepted truths, urging readers to dissect the real motivations behind global conflicts. To understand the philosophy of war propaganda, Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, defines key concepts such as "manufactured consent," "psychological warfare," and "strategic misinformation." The book provides an analytical framework to decipher how propaganda functions across different political systems and historical periods. Truth becomes a malleable instrument in the hands of those who control information. The book dissects how linguistic framing, emotional appeal, and repetition are used to construct compelling war narratives that suppress critical thinking and pacify opposition. The modern world presents an evolution in propaganda techniques. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, highlights the role of digital warfare, social media manipulation, and the emergence of artificial intelligence-driven disinformation campaigns. Governments and non-state actors alike now have unprecedented tools to shape perceptions on a global scale. Case studies illustrate how recent conflicts have been fueled by misinformation, fabricated threats, and the demonization of opponents. The book presents chilling examples of how media, once seen as a guardian of truth, often becomes complicit in amplifying war rhetoric. This book is built upon principles that deconstruct the political philosophy of propaganda. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, adopts an interdisciplinary approach, integrating political science, psychology, and media studies to expose how war narratives are crafted and sustained. Through a comparative analysis of historical and contemporary conflicts, the book establishes a framework to recognize and challenge propaganda in real time. The goal is not just to understand the phenomenon but to empower individuals and institutions to resist its influence. To assess the presence and impact of war propaganda, this book identifies recurring indicators, including: • The deliberate distortion of facts to justify military action. • The portrayal of war as an act of moral duty or national survival. • The suppression of dissenting voices through censorship or intimidation. • The glorification of military actions while downplaying civilian casualties. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, meticulously examines these elements, providing readers with analytical tools to recognize propaganda before it takes hold. The effectiveness of war propaganda is influenced by several operational variables, which include state control over media, public education, and ideological indoctrination. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, reveals how these variables intersect to create a cohesive and persuasive narrative that discourages critical scrutiny. A crucial aspect of this analysis is the role of education as both a target and a solution. The book explores how school curricula, history books, and public discourse shape perceptions of war from an early age. The persistence of war propaganda is driven by key determinant factors such as: • The geopolitical interests of states seeking to expand influence. • The economic benefits of sustained military conflicts. • The ideological rivalries that create perpetual divisions. • The complicity of mass media in disseminating misleading information. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, argues that these factors create a self-reinforcing system that ensures propaganda remains a powerful force in global politics. While propaganda is deeply entrenched in political structures, strategies exist to counter its effects. The book proposes reforms in education, media literacy programs, and international regulations on misinformation. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, emphasizes the importance of academic institutions and global organizations in fostering a more informed and critically engaged society. The role of The Education Training Centre is examined as a model for institutions dedicated to cultivating critical thinking and resistance to manipulative narratives. Efforts to dismantle propaganda face resistance from state entities, corporate media interests, and political ideologues who benefit from maintaining control over information. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, acknowledges these challenges while also highlighting the growing movement of independent journalism and grassroots educational initiatives pushing back against misinformation. The book closes with a sobering yet hopeful message. Prof. Dr. Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad, Ph.D., DBA, asserts that propaganda will always exist, but its power depends on the willingness of societies to accept it without question. By cultivating skepticism, promoting transparency, and demanding accountability, humanity can reclaim its autonomy from those who seek to manipulate truth for political gain.
